warmup.q: A MutableStateFlow<Int>(0) has one collector that takes 100 ms per value. Code sets value = 1, 2 and 3 within a millisecond, and later sets 3 again. Which values does the collector see?
options: Only 3, because the collector started late
warmup.why: A StateFlow holds one current value. A busy collector doesn't get a queue of what it missed; it gets the latest value when it is ready, so 1 and 2 are skipped. Setting a value equal to the current one does nothing at all, so the second 3 never arrives.

sections.h: StateFlow is one current value, and it skips what you missed
sections.html:
A StateFlow<T> always has a value. You can read it with .value at any moment, and when you collect it you get the current value first, then each new one. It is hot: it exists and holds its value whether or not anyone collects, unlike the cold flows of lesson 7 of this track. That makes it the natural type for state such as a payment's status, a circuit breaker's state or the latest FX rate.

Java
// Java equivalent: a Reactor sink that replays its latest value, with repeats filtered out
Sinks.Many<PaymentStatus> status = Sinks.many().replay().latestOrDefault(PaymentStatus.PENDING);
status.tryEmitNext(PaymentStatus.AUTHORIZED);
status.asFlux().distinctUntilChanged().subscribe(this::render);
Kotlin
val status = MutableStateFlow(PaymentStatus.PENDING)
status.value = PaymentStatus.AUTHORIZED     // set from any thread
println(status.value)                       // AUTHORIZED
status.collect { render(it) }               // current value first, then each change; never returns

Two rules make StateFlow cheap, and both surprise people. Updates are conflated: a slow collector doesn't get a queue of the values it missed, it gets the latest one when it is ready. Set 1, 2 and 3 in quick succession while a collector is busy and it sees 3 next, never 1 or 2. And it compares with equals. Setting a value equal to the current one does nothing, and no collector wakes up. With a data class, a new object with the same fields counts as equal.

Both rules follow from what StateFlow is. Its KDoc describes MutableStateFlow(initial) as a shared flow with replay = 1 and DROP_OLDEST, seeded with the initial value and followed by distinctUntilChanged().

So StateFlow is for state, where only the latest value matters. It is the wrong type for events, where every one matters: payment transitions for the audit log, "send this receipt" commands, ledger postings. Conflation would drop some of them without a trace. Events need SharedFlow, which is the next section.

One more thing to expect: collect on a StateFlow never returns. The KDoc says it plainly, "state flow never completes". Collect it in a coroutine you will cancel, or wait for one particular value with first: status.first { it == PaymentStatus.CAPTURED }.

code.title: StateFlowConflation.kt
code.html: package workbench.coroutines.l08 import kotlinx.coroutines.CoroutineStart import kotlinx.coroutines.delay import kotlinx.coroutines.flow.MutableStateFlow import kotlinx.coroutines.launch import kotlinx.coroutines.runBlocking data class Rate(val pair: String, val mid: Double) fun main() = runBlocking { val eurUsd = MutableStateFlow(Rate("EUR/USD", 1.0809)) val dashboard = launch(start = CoroutineStart.UNDISPATCHED) { eurUsd.collect { rate -> println("dashboard shows ${rate.mid}") delay(100) // rendering is slow } } // three ticks arrive while the dashboard is busy rendering the first value eurUsd.value = Rate("EUR/USD", 1.0811) eurUsd.value = Rate("EUR/USD", 1.0812) eurUsd.value = Rate("EUR/USD", 1.0813) delay(150) println("setting an equal rate again (a new object, same fields)") eurUsd.value = Rate("EUR/USD", 1.0813) delay(150) println("value is ${eurUsd.value.mid}; the collector is still waiting, because a StateFlow never completes") dashboard.cancel() }

alt.title: StateFlowConflationJava.java
alt.html: // Java equivalent of StateFlowConflation.kt with Reactor: a sink that replays its latest value, // distinctUntilChanged for the equality rule, and onBackpressureLatest so a slow subscriber only // gets the newest value. StateFlow does all three by itself. package workbench.coroutines.l08; import reactor.core.Disposable; import reactor.core.publisher.Sinks; import reactor.core.scheduler.Schedulers; public class StateFlowConflationJava { record Rate(String pair, double mid) {} public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException { Sinks.Many<Rate> eurUsd = Sinks.many().replay().latestOrDefault(new Rate("EUR/USD", 1.0809)); Disposable dashboard = eurUsd.asFlux() .distinctUntilChanged() .onBackpressureLatest() .publishOn(Schedulers.single(), 1) // request one value at a time .subscribe(rate -> { System.out.println("dashboard shows " + rate.mid()); sleep(100); // rendering is slow }); Thread.sleep(20); // three ticks arrive while the dashboard is busy rendering the first value eurUsd.tryEmitNext(new Rate("EUR/USD", 1.0811)); eurUsd.tryEmitNext(new Rate("EUR/USD", 1.0812)); eurUsd.tryEmitNext(new Rate("EUR/USD", 1.0813)); Thread.sleep(250); System.out.println("setting an equal rate again (a new object, same fields)"); eurUsd.tryEmitNext(new Rate("EUR/USD", 1.0813)); Thread.sleep(150); dashboard.dispose(); } static void sleep(long ms) { try { Thread.sleep(ms); } catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); } } }

try.expect: The dashboard shows 1.0809, then 1.0813: the two ticks in between are skipped. Setting the equal rate again prints nothing. With a plain class, equality falls back to identity, so the "equal" rate is a new value and the dashboard shows 1.0813 a second time. The Java twin prints the same two lines, using replay().latestOrDefault, distinctUntilChanged and onBackpressureLatest.

sections.h: SharedFlow is for events, and its buffer decides what gets lost
sections.html:
A MutableSharedFlow<T> broadcasts every value to every current subscriber. It has no current value. Three parameters decide what it keeps:

Java
// Java equivalent: a multicast Reactor sink with a buffer for slow subscribers
Sinks.Many<Transition> transitions = Sinks.many().multicast().onBackpressureBuffer(64, false);
Sinks.EmitResult result = transitions.tryEmitNext(t);   // FAIL_OVERFLOW when full
Kotlin
val transitions = MutableSharedFlow<Transition>(
    replay = 0,                                 // late subscribers get no history
    extraBufferCapacity = 64,                   // room for values a slow subscriber hasn't read yet
    onBufferOverflow = BufferOverflow.SUSPEND,  // when full: emit waits, tryEmit returns false
)

replay is how many recent values a new subscriber gets first. extraBufferCapacity is room beyond that for values that slow subscribers haven't taken yet. onBufferOverflow decides what happens when all of it is full. SUSPEND, the default, makes emit wait for the slowest subscriber. DROP_OLDEST throws away the oldest buffered value, and DROP_LATEST throws away the new one. The two drop policies need some replay or buffer to work with.

emit is a suspend function. tryEmit is its non-suspending twin for code that can't suspend, such as a Kafka listener callback, and it returns false when the value doesn't fit. Here is the trap. With the default parameters there is no buffer at all, so tryEmit fails whenever a subscriber is busy, and the value is lost unless you check the result. The lab's stub has exactly this bug. Give the flow a buffer, and check what tryEmit returns.

A SharedFlow never completes either, and a value emitted while nobody subscribes goes nowhere, apart from the replay cache. If events must survive having no listener, you want something else: a Channel with one consumer (lesson 9 of this track), or a durable topic.

Put side by side: StateFlow has a value, replays exactly one, conflates and skips duplicates. SharedFlow has no value, replays what you configure, and with a buffer and SUSPEND it delivers every event to every subscriber. Both are safe to emit into from many threads at once. Reactor's sinks are not by default: concurrent tryEmitNext calls can fail with FAIL_NON_SERIALIZED.

try.title: Find out which events get through
steps: Read SharedFlowEvents.kt. Each case calls tryEmit five times while the only subscriber needs 50 ms per event. Predict the five results and what is received, for each of the four configurations.
Run it.
Change the last case to MutableSharedFlow(replay = 1, extraBufferCapacity = 64). Does anything in that line change?
Run the Java twin.

code.title: SharedFlowEvents.kt
code.html: package workbench.coroutines.l08 import kotlinx.coroutines.CoroutineStart import kotlinx.coroutines.channels.BufferOverflow import kotlinx.coroutines.delay import kotlinx.coroutines.flow.MutableSharedFlow import kotlinx.coroutines.launch import kotlinx.coroutines.runBlocking /** Emits five events with tryEmit while one subscriber is busy, and reports what got through. */ suspend fun tryFive(label: String, events: MutableSharedFlow<String>) = kotlinx.coroutines.coroutineScope { val received = mutableListOf<String>() val auditor = launch(start = CoroutineStart.UNDISPATCHED) { events.collect { delay(50); received += it } // the audit write takes 50 ms } val accepted = (1..5).map { events.tryEmit("e$it") } delay(400) auditor.cancel() println("%-40s tryEmit: %s received: %s".format(label, accepted, received)) } fun main() = runBlocking { tryFive("default (no replay, no buffer)", MutableSharedFlow()) tryFive("extraBufferCapacity = 2", MutableSharedFlow(extraBufferCapacity = 2)) tryFive("extraBufferCapacity = 2, DROP_OLDEST", MutableSharedFlow(extraBufferCapacity = 2, onBufferOverflow = BufferOverflow.DROP_OLDEST)) tryFive("extraBufferCapacity = 64", MutableSharedFlow(extraBufferCapacity = 64)) // replay: what a subscriber that arrives later gets first val replayed = MutableSharedFlow<String>(replay = 2) (1..5).forEach { replayed.emit("e$it") } // no subscribers yet println("a late subscriber to replay = 2 first gets: ${replayed.replayCache}") }

alt.title: SharedFlowEventsJava.java
alt.html: // Java equivalent of SharedFlowEvents.kt with Reactor sinks: a multicast sink with a bounded // buffer refuses values when a slow subscriber can't keep up (FAIL_OVERFLOW instead of false), // and a replay sink keeps the last N values for late subscribers. Reactor sizes small buffers up // to its own minimum, so this twin sends 20 events instead of 5 to fill one. package workbench.coroutines.l08; import java.util.ArrayList; import java.util.List; import java.util.concurrent.CopyOnWriteArrayList; import reactor.core.Disposable; import reactor.core.publisher.Sinks; import reactor.core.scheduler.Schedulers; public class SharedFlowEventsJava { static void tryTwenty(String label, Sinks.Many<String> events) throws InterruptedException { List<String> received = new CopyOnWriteArrayList<>(); Disposable auditor = events.asFlux() .publishOn(Schedulers.single(), 1) .subscribe(e -> { sleep(50); received.add(e); }); // the audit write takes 50 ms List<Sinks.EmitResult> results = new ArrayList<>(); for (int i = 1; i <= 20; i++) results.add(events.tryEmitNext("e" + i)); Thread.sleep(1_200); auditor.dispose(); long ok = results.stream().filter(r -> r == Sinks.EmitResult.OK).count(); System.out.printf("%-26s tryEmitNext OK: %2d, FAIL_OVERFLOW: %2d received %2d events%n", label, ok, results.size() - ok, received.size()); } public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException { tryTwenty("multicast, buffer of 2", Sinks.many().multicast().onBackpressureBuffer(2, false)); tryTwenty("multicast, buffer of 64", Sinks.many().multicast().onBackpressureBuffer(64, false)); Sinks.Many<String> replayed = Sinks.many().replay().limit(2); for (int i = 1; i <= 5; i++) replayed.tryEmitNext("e" + i); // no subscribers yet List<String> late = new ArrayList<>(); replayed.asFlux().subscribe(late::add).dispose(); System.out.println("a late subscriber to replay().limit(2) first gets: " + late); } static void sleep(long ms) { try { Thread.sleep(ms); } catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); } } }

try.expect: Default: [false, false, false, false, false] and nothing received: no room at all while the subscriber is busy. Buffer of 2: two true, then false, and [e1, e2] received. Buffer of 2 with DROP_OLDEST: every tryEmit returns true, but only [e4, e5] arrive, because the older ones were dropped. Buffer of 64: everything gets through. The late subscriber to replay = 2 gets [e4, e5]. Adding replay = 1 changes nothing in that line: the subscriber was there from the start. The Java twin reports FAIL_OVERFLOW instead of false, and only after 9 events, because Reactor rounds small buffers up.

sections.h: Turn one cold flow into a shared hot one with stateIn and shareIn
sections.html:
A cold flow runs once per collector. If three ops dashboards each collect a flow that polls the acquirer's settlement API, the API is polled three times. stateIn and shareIn run the upstream once, in a scope you give them, and share its values:

Java
// Java equivalent: one shared upstream that starts with the first subscriber
// and stops 5 seconds after the last one leaves
Flux<Long> capturedTotal = captures
    .scan(0L, Long::sum)
    .replay(1)
    .refCount(1, Duration.ofSeconds(5));
Kotlin
val capturedTotal: StateFlow<Long> = captures            // a cold flow fed from Kafka
    .runningFold(0L) { total, cents -> total + cents }
    .stateIn(scope, SharingStarted.WhileSubscribed(5_000), initialValue = 0L)

stateIn gives a StateFlow, so it needs an initial value. shareIn(scope, started, replay) gives a SharedFlow. The started argument decides when the shared upstream runs:

  • SharingStarted.Eagerly starts at once, before any subscriber, and runs until the scope is cancelled.
  • SharingStarted.Lazily starts with the first subscriber and then never stops.
  • SharingStarted.WhileSubscribed(stopTimeoutMillis) starts with the first subscriber and stops once the last one has been gone for stopTimeoutMillis. The default is 0. A few seconds is common, so a page reload or a quick reconnect doesn't restart the upstream.

The scope owns the shared collection, so make it a long-lived scope you control, like the owned scopes of lesson 3 of this track. A request's scope would end the sharing when the request ends, and GlobalScope would never end it. In tests, backgroundScope plays that part.

There is also a suspend overload, stateIn(scope) without started, which waits for the first value and keeps the upstream running for the life of the scope.

Sharing doesn't make the upstream any less cold. When WhileSubscribed stops it and a new subscriber arrives later, the upstream runs again from the top: the poll loop restarts, and a runningFold starts again from its initial value. That is usually what you want for a live feed. For a total that must survive restarts, keep it somewhere durable and use the flow only to show it.

code.title: StateInDemo.kt
code.html: package workbench.coroutines.l08 import kotlinx.coroutines.CoroutineScope import kotlinx.coroutines.Dispatchers import kotlinx.coroutines.SupervisorJob import kotlinx.coroutines.cancel import kotlinx.coroutines.delay import kotlinx.coroutines.flow.SharingStarted import kotlinx.coroutines.flow.flow import kotlinx.coroutines.flow.onCompletion import kotlinx.coroutines.flow.onStart import kotlinx.coroutines.flow.stateIn import kotlinx.coroutines.launch import kotlinx.coroutines.runBlocking private var t0 = 0L private fun at(msg: String) = println("%5d ms %s".format((System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000, msg)) fun main(args: Array<String>) = runBlocking { t0 = System.nanoTime() val started = when (args.firstOrNull()) { "eagerly" -> SharingStarted.Eagerly "lazily" -> SharingStarted.Lazily else -> SharingStarted.WhileSubscribed(stopTimeoutMillis = 300) } // a cold flow that polls the FX provider every 100 ms val polls = flow { var n = 0 while (true) { emit(1.0800 + n++ / 10_000.0); delay(100) } }.onStart { at("upstream: polling started") }.onCompletion { at("upstream: polling stopped") } val appScope = CoroutineScope(SupervisorJob() + Dispatchers.Default) // the owner of the sharing val rate = polls.stateIn(appScope, started, initialValue = 0.0) at("stateIn returned; waiting 200 ms before the first dashboard") delay(200) val a = launch { rate.collect { } } val b = launch { rate.collect { } } at("two dashboards subscribed") delay(250) a.cancel(); b.cancel() at("both dashboards left; rate.value = ${rate.value}") delay(500) at("done") appScope.cancel() }

alt.title: StateInDemoJava.java
alt.html: // Java equivalent of StateInDemo.kt with Reactor: replay(1).refCount(1, grace) shares one // upstream between subscribers, starts it with the first one, and stops it when the last one // has been gone for the grace period, like stateIn with WhileSubscribed(300). package workbench.coroutines.l08; import java.time.Duration; import reactor.core.Disposable; import reactor.core.publisher.Flux; public class StateInDemoJava { static long t0; static void at(String msg) { System.out.printf("%5d ms %s%n", (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000, msg); } public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException { t0 = System.nanoTime(); // a cold flux that polls the FX provider every 100 ms Flux<Double> polls = Flux.interval(Duration.ZERO, Duration.ofMillis(100)) .map(n -> 1.0800 + n / 10_000.0) .doOnSubscribe(s -> at("upstream: polling started")) .doOnCancel(() -> at("upstream: polling stopped")); Flux<Double> rate = polls.replay(1).refCount(1, Duration.ofMillis(300)); at("refCount returned; waiting 200 ms before the first dashboard"); Thread.sleep(200); Disposable a = rate.subscribe(); Disposable b = rate.subscribe(); at("two dashboards subscribed"); Thread.sleep(250); a.dispose(); b.dispose(); at("both dashboards left"); Thread.sleep(500); at("done"); } }

try.expect: With WhileSubscribed(300), polling starts only when the dashboards subscribe, at about 200 ms, once for both. It stops about 300 ms after they leave. With eagerly, polling starts at once, before anyone subscribes, and stops only when the scope is cancelled at the end. With lazily, it starts with the first dashboard and never stops on its own. The Java twin starts and stops at the same moments as the WhileSubscribed run.

sections.h: Keep the mutable flow private and update it in one step
sections.html:
A class that owns some state should let callers read it and nobody else write it. Before Kotlin 2.4 that took two properties:

Java
// Java equivalent: a private sink and a public read-only view
class PaymentTracker {
    private final Sinks.Many<PaymentStatus> status = Sinks.many().replay().latestOrDefault(PaymentStatus.PENDING);

    public Flux<PaymentStatus> status() { return status.asFlux(); }

    void authorize() { status.tryEmitNext(PaymentStatus.AUTHORIZED); }
}
Kotlin
class PaymentTracker {
    private val _status = MutableStateFlow(PaymentStatus.PENDING)
    val status: StateFlow<PaymentStatus> = _status.asStateFlow()

    fun authorize() { _status.value = PaymentStatus.AUTHORIZED }
}

Kotlin 2.4.0 made explicit backing fields stable. They arrived as experimental in 2.3.0, whose release notes used exactly this case as their example. One property declares its public type and, separately, its field:

class PaymentTracker {
    val status: StateFlow<PaymentStatus>
        field = MutableStateFlow(PaymentStatus.PENDING)

    fun authorize() { status.value = PaymentStatus.AUTHORIZED }   // smart-cast inside the class
}

Outside the class, status is a StateFlow with no setter. Inside it, the compiler knows the field is a MutableStateFlow and smart-casts. One small difference remains. asStateFlow() returns a wrapper, so a caller can't cast it back to MutableStateFlow. An explicit backing field hides the type only at compile time. Both are fine in application code. In a library other teams build on, the wrapper is the stricter choice.

Then write every change as one atomic step. count.value = count.value + 1 is a read-modify-write (lesson 3 of the threads track), and two threads running it together lose updates. count.update { it + 1 } retries with compare-and-set until it wins. status.compareAndSet(expected, new) moves only if the value is still expected and returns whether it did. That is how the lab's tracker makes sure two Kafka listener threads can't both capture the same payment: the loser's compareAndSet fails, it reads the new status, and the move is no longer allowed.

The same habit applies to SharedFlow events. Emit from the method that changes the state, after the change has succeeded, so the event stream never describes a move that didn't happen.

try.title: Lose cents with value = value + 1
steps: Read StateUpdates.kt. Eight coroutines on Default each add a cent 100,000 times. Predict both totals.
Run it twice.
Run the Java twin, which does the same with an AtomicReference.

code.title: StateUpdates.kt
code.html: package workbench.coroutines.l08 import kotlinx.coroutines.Dispatchers import kotlinx.coroutines.coroutineScope import kotlinx.coroutines.flow.MutableStateFlow import kotlinx.coroutines.flow.update import kotlinx.coroutines.launch import kotlinx.coroutines.runBlocking /** 8 coroutines on Default each add 1 cent to a shared StateFlow 100,000 times. */ suspend fun addCents(label: String, add: (MutableStateFlow<Long>) -> Unit) { val capturedCents = MutableStateFlow(0L) coroutineScope { repeat(8) { launch(Dispatchers.Default) { repeat(100_000) { add(capturedCents) } } } } println("%-34s expected 800000, got %d".format(label, capturedCents.value)) } fun main() = runBlocking { addCents("value = value + 1") { it.value = it.value + 1 } // read-modify-write: loses updates addCents("update { it + 1 }") { it.update { cents -> cents + 1 } } // compare-and-set in a loop }

alt.title: StateUpdatesJava.java
alt.html: // Java equivalent of StateUpdates.kt: the same read-modify-write race on an AtomicReference, // fixed the same way, with a compare-and-set loop (updateAndGet). package workbench.coroutines.l08; import java.util.concurrent.ExecutorService; import java.util.concurrent.Executors; import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicReference; import java.util.function.Consumer; public class StateUpdatesJava { static void addCents(String label, Consumer<AtomicReference<Long>> add) { AtomicReference<Long> capturedCents = new AtomicReference<>(0L); try (ExecutorService pool = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(8)) { for (int t = 0; t < 8; t++) pool.submit(() -> { for (int i = 0; i < 100_000; i++) add.accept(capturedCents); }); } System.out.printf("%-34s expected 800000, got %d%n", label, capturedCents.get()); } public static void main(String[] args) { addCents("set(get() + 1)", ref -> ref.set(ref.get() + 1)); // read-modify-write: loses updates addCents("updateAndGet(c -> c + 1)", ref -> ref.updateAndGet(c -> c + 1)); // compare-and-set in a loop } }

try.expect: value = value + 1 comes out far short of 800,000, and the number changes from run to run (one run here gave 259,299). update { it + 1 } gives exactly 800,000 every time. The Java twin loses updates with set(get() + 1) and gets 800,000 with updateAndGet, because they are the same race and the same fix.

refs.title: What's new in Kotlin 2.4.0 (explicit backing fields)

analogy: A StateFlow is the departures board at a station. It always shows something, it shows only the latest state of each train, and if you look away while a platform changes twice, you see only the final platform. Nobody announces "still on time" again. A SharedFlow is the station's public address system. Every announcement goes to everyone standing there, people who arrive late hear nothing that was said before they came (unless the station repeats the last few, which is replay), and if the announcer talks faster than the slowest listener can follow, someone has to wait or a message gets cut. stateIn is putting one person in charge of phoning the control room and updating the board for everyone, instead of every passenger phoning in. The analogy breaks at the empty station: a real announcer stops talking when nobody is there, but a SharedFlow's emitter keeps going, and the announcements simply vanish.
world: In a payment service, StateFlow fits anything a page or a health check reads as "the current value": a payment's status for the status endpoint, the circuit breaker in front of the card issuer, the latest FX rates. SharedFlow fits in-process events, such as status transitions that an audit writer and a notifier both consume. Remember it is in memory only: an audit trail that must survive a pod restart still belongs in Kafka or an outbox table, with the SharedFlow as a fast in-process fan-out at most. Kafka listener threads can't suspend, so they publish with tryEmit, which means the flow needs a buffer and the result must be checked or turned into a metric. For a live ops dashboard or a server-sent-events endpoint in Quarkus, stateIn(appScope, WhileSubscribed(5_000), initial) gives every open connection the same feed from one upstream, and stops polling when nobody is watching.
mistake: The most common mistake is using a StateFlow (or MutableSharedFlow() with default parameters) as an event bus. With StateFlow, two transitions in quick succession arrive as one, and repeating an event that equals the current value delivers nothing, so an audit log quietly misses entries. With a default SharedFlow, tryEmit from a non-suspending callback returns false whenever a subscriber is busy, and the event vanishes. Both look fine in a unit test with one fast collector. Decide what the stream carries. State, where only the latest matters, goes in a StateFlow. Events, where every one matters, go in a SharedFlow with extraBufferCapacity sized for bursts, SUSPEND overflow, and a checked tryEmit (or emit from a coroutine).

compare.title: A payment tracker: Reactor sinks vs StateFlow and SharedFlow

java.title: PaymentTracker.java
java.html: class PaymentTracker { private final AtomicReference<PaymentStatus> current = new AtomicReference<>(PaymentStatus.PENDING); private final Sinks.Many<PaymentStatus> status = Sinks.many().replay().latestOrDefault(PaymentStatus.PENDING); private final Sinks.Many<Transition> transitions = Sinks.many().multicast().onBackpressureBuffer(64, false); public PaymentStatus currentStatus() { return current.get(); } // 1. a synchronous read public Flux<PaymentStatus> status() { return status.asFlux().distinctUntilChanged(); } public Flux<Transition> transitions() { return transitions.asFlux(); } boolean moveTo(PaymentStatus next) { PaymentStatus from = current.get(); if (!from.canMoveTo(next) || !current.compareAndSet(from, next)) return false; // 2. atomic move // 3. sinks reject concurrent emits (FAIL_NON_SERIALIZED), so serialize them synchronized (this) { status.tryEmitNext(next); transitions.tryEmitNext(new Transition(id, from, next)); } return true; } }

kotlin.title: PaymentTracker.kt
kotlin.html: class PaymentTracker(private val id: String) { val status: StateFlow<PaymentStatus> // 1. .value is a synchronous read field = MutableStateFlow(PaymentStatus.PENDING) val transitions: SharedFlow<Transition> field = MutableSharedFlow(extraBufferCapacity = 64) fun moveTo(next: PaymentStatus): Boolean { while (true) { val from = status.value if (!from.canMoveTo(next)) return false if (status.compareAndSet(from, next)) { // 2. atomic move check(transitions.tryEmit(Transition(id, from, next))) // 3. safe from any thread return true } } } }

compare.note: The Kotlin version needs fewer moving parts because StateFlow is both the holder and the stream: .value reads it synchronously, compareAndSet changes it atomically, and collectors see changes with conflation and de-duplication built in. Reactor has no single type for that, so the Java version keeps an AtomicReference for the value and a replaying sink for the stream, and must keep them consistent. The other real difference is concurrency. MutableStateFlow and MutableSharedFlow are documented as safe for concurrent emitters. Reactor's default sinks detect concurrent tryEmitNext calls and fail them with FAIL_NON_SERIALIZED, so the Java tracker serializes its emits.

worked.title: Share one FX feed across every dashboard

steps.say: An ops dashboard shows live FX rates over server-sent events. Each open connection collects rates(), a cold flow that polls the provider every second. With 40 open tabs the provider sees 40 polls a second and starts rate-limiting the payment service too.
steps.code: fun rates(): Flow<FxRates> = flow { while (true) { emit(provider.latest()) // one HTTP call per collector per second delay(1.seconds) } } // in the SSE resource, once per connection rates().collect { send(it) }

alt.html: // Java equivalent of the same design: a cold Flux subscribed once per connection Flux<FxRates> rates() { return Flux.interval(Duration.ZERO, Duration.ofSeconds(1)) .concatMap(tick -> provider.latest()); // one HTTP call per subscriber per second } // in the SSE resource, once per connection return rates();

steps.say: Decide the type first. A dashboard wants the latest rates, and a tab that missed a tick doesn't need it replayed, so this is state: a StateFlow.
Share the upstream in a scope that lives as long as the service, and stop it when nobody watches. Five seconds of grace covers a tab reload.
steps.code: @ApplicationScoped class FxFeed(provider: FxProvider) : AutoCloseable { private val scope = CoroutineScope(SupervisorJob() + Dispatchers.IO) // 1. the owner of the sharing val rates: StateFlow<FxRates?> = flow { while (true) { emit(provider.latest()); delay(1.seconds) } }.stateIn(scope, SharingStarted.WhileSubscribed(5_000), initialValue = null) // 2. one poll for all override fun close() = scope.cancel() // 3. ends with the bean }

alt.html: @ApplicationScoped class FxFeed { // 1. and 2.: one shared poll, started by the first subscriber, stopped 5 s after the last final Flux<FxRates> rates; FxFeed(FxProvider provider) { this.rates = Flux.interval(Duration.ZERO, Duration.ofSeconds(1)) .concatMap(tick -> provider.latest()) .replay(1) .refCount(1, Duration.ofSeconds(5)); } }

steps.say: Each connection now collects the shared StateFlow. A slow client gets the newest rates rather than a backlog, and a tick with unchanged rates (an equal data class) isn't sent at all.
steps.code: // in the SSE resource, once per connection: no extra poll fxFeed.rates.filterNotNull().collect { send(it) }

alt.html: // in the SSE resource, once per connection: no extra poll return fxFeed.rates.distinctUntilChanged().onBackpressureLatest();

steps.say: Self-check: why not SharingStarted.Eagerly? (It would poll the provider every second from startup, even at night with no dashboards open, and never stop until shutdown. WhileSubscribed polls only while someone is watching.)

lab.title: A payment tracker and a live total
steps: Run the tests. Five of seven fail. PaymentStatus.kt has the allowed moves; PaymentTracker.kt already uses explicit backing fields, so status is read-only outside the class.
Give transitions a buffer: MutableSharedFlow(replay = 0, extraBufferCapacity = 64). The two transition tests should pass.

Make moveTo atomic: in a loop, read status.value, check canMoveTo, call beforeMove, then status.compareAndSet(from, next). If the CAS fails, go round again. Emit the transition only after a successful CAS.
In LiveTotals.kt, replace SharingStarted.Eagerly with SharingStarted.WhileSubscribed(stopTimeoutMillis = 5_000).
Run the tests until all seven pass.
hints: Inside the class, status smart-casts to MutableStateFlow, so status.compareAndSet(from, next) and transitions.tryEmit(...) compile without a cast.
Check what tryEmit returns. With a buffer of 64 it should always be true here; check(...) turns a surprise false into a loud failure instead of a lost event.
The race test holds both threads in beforeMove until both have read AUTHORIZED. With compareAndSet, the second one's CAS fails, it reads CAPTURED, and canMoveTo says no.
The stateIn tests run on virtual time, so WhileSubscribed(5_000) takes no real time at all.

drill.title: A circuit breaker's state, from memory
drill.prompt: Close this page. Write class IssuerBreaker with a read-only state: StateFlow<BreakerState> (CLOSED at first) backed by a mutable one, fun trip(): Boolean that moves CLOSED to OPEN atomically and returns whether this call did it, and events: SharedFlow<String> that a non-suspending caller can publish to with tryEmit even while a subscriber is busy.

answer.html: class IssuerBreaker { val state: StateFlow<BreakerState> field = MutableStateFlow(BreakerState.CLOSED) val events: SharedFlow<String> field = MutableSharedFlow(extraBufferCapacity = 64) fun trip(): Boolean { if (!state.compareAndSet(BreakerState.CLOSED, BreakerState.OPEN)) return false check(events.tryEmit("breaker opened")) return true } }

alt.title: Java equivalent
alt.html: // Java equivalent: an atomic holder for the state, a buffered multicast sink for events class IssuerBreaker { private final AtomicReference<BreakerState> state = new AtomicReference<>(BreakerState.CLOSED); private final Sinks.Many<String> events = Sinks.many().multicast().onBackpressureBuffer(64, false); BreakerState state() { return state.get(); } Flux<String> events() { return events.asFlux(); } synchronized boolean trip() { // synchronized: Reactor sinks reject concurrent emits if (!state.compareAndSet(BreakerState.CLOSED, BreakerState.OPEN)) return false; events.tryEmitNext("breaker opened").orThrow(); return true; } }

recap: A StateFlow is hot and always has a value. It conflates (slow collectors get only the latest) and skips values equal to the current one, so it is for state, not events.
A SharedFlow broadcasts every value to every subscriber. replay is history for late subscribers, extraBufferCapacity is room for slow ones, and onBufferOverflow says what happens when both are full.
With default parameters a MutableSharedFlow has no buffer, so tryEmit fails while a subscriber is busy. Give it a buffer and check the result.
stateIn and shareIn run a cold upstream once in a scope you own and share it. WhileSubscribed(stopTimeoutMillis) starts with the first subscriber and stops after the last one has left.
Expose state read-only with an explicit backing field (val s: StateFlow<T> with field = MutableStateFlow(...), stable since Kotlin 2.4) or asStateFlow().
Change shared state in one atomic step: update { } or compareAndSet, never value = value + 1.

explain.prompt: A teammate stores payment transitions in a MutableStateFlow<Transition?> so the audit writer can collect them, and the audit log is missing entries under load. Explain why, and what you would use instead.
explain.answer: A StateFlow holds one current value, so it's built to drop history. When the audit writer is busy writing one transition and two more happen, it only gets the latest one when it's ready, and the middle one is gone. It also skips a value equal to the current one, so a repeated transition never arrives. That's right for state like "the current status", but transitions are events and every one matters. I'd use a MutableSharedFlow with no replay and an extraBufferCapacity big enough for bursts, keep the default SUSPEND overflow, and check what tryEmit returns from the Kafka threads so a full buffer shows up as an error instead of a lost entry. And because it's all in memory, anything that must survive a restart should also go to the outbox table or a Kafka topic.

deeper.html:
MutableSharedFlow has a subscriptionCount: StateFlow<Int>. It is deliberately not conflated, so you can react to the first subscriber arriving or the last one leaving, for example to open and close a connection to a market-data feed. SharingStarted is an interface, and WhileSubscribed is written on top of exactly that count. A custom strategy can start sharing only during business hours, or only after a warm-up.

WhileSubscribed has a second parameter, replayExpirationMillis, which defaults to Long.MAX_VALUE. It decides how long the last value stays in the replay cache after the upstream stops. Set it to 0 if a stale value is worse than none, for instance a rate that must never be shown once its feed is down.

stateIn and shareIn keep a coroutine running in the scope you give them, so the scope's lifetime is the sharing's lifetime. If the upstream throws, that coroutine fails, the error goes up into the scope, and the StateFlow simply stops updating. Put a catch or retryWhen on the upstream, above stateIn, and decide what the subscribers should see while it recovers.

kotlinx.coroutines 1.11 added two small helpers. SharedFlow.asFlow() returns a view that hides the hot-flow type, so callers can't rely on it being shared. And there is now an onSubscription overload on StateFlow that keeps the StateFlow type. Kotlin 2.1.20 also added common atomics such as AtomicInt in kotlin.concurrent.atomics, marked experimental. For plain counters shared between coroutines they are an alternative to a StateFlow you never collect, which lesson 10 of this track compares with Mutex.
